content: The law of conservation of mass, also referred to as the law of mass or matter conservation, states that within a closed system, the total mass remains constant regardless of the processes occurring within the system. This principle asserts that matter cannot be created or destroyed, though it can undergo rearrangement. Consequently, in any chemical reaction occurring in a closed system, the total mass of the reactants must be equal to the total mass of the products. However, this law, when interpreted as the conservation of particles, is an approximation that holds true only in the classical framework, prior to the development of special relativity and quantum mechanics. In open systems, where energy can enter or leave, mass is not generally conserved. Nevertheless, in modern physics, the conservation of mass for closed systems, as observed from their center of momentum inertial frames, remains valid. This concept has been historically significant and is extensively applied in fields such as chemistry, mechanics, and fluid dynamics. In the historical context, an early but incomplete version of the conservation of mass was proposed by Nasīr al-Dīn al-Tūsī in the 13th century. He suggested that matter could change form but could not vanish. The law was formally articulated by Antoine Lavoisier in 1789, earning him recognition as a father of modern chemistry. However, Mikhail Lomonosov had already expressed similar ideas in 1748 and supported them with experimental evidence. Other scientists, such as Joseph Black, Henry Cavendish, and Jean Rey, also anticipated Lavoisier’s work. For centuries, the understanding of mass conservation was obscured by the buoyant effects of the Earth’s atmosphere on the weight of gases, a phenomenon that was not fully understood until the invention of the vacuum pump allowed for accurate weighing of gases. Once this effect was accounted for, the principle of mass conservation became pivotal in transforming alchemy into modern chemistry. Scientists realized that substances did not disappear during chemical reactions, enabling them to conduct quantitative studies of substance transformations. This led to the identification of chemical elements and the understanding that all chemical reactions involve fixed amounts or weights of these elements. The law of conservation of mass remains a cornerstone of scientific inquiry worldwide. In the framework of special relativity, the conservation of mass does not hold in the same way as in classical physics. The classical principle that the total mass of a system of particles equals the sum of their individual masses is not valid in relativistic contexts. According to the mass-energy equivalence principle, bound systems have a mass that is less than the sum of their constituent parts. This discrepancy, known as the mass defect, reflects the binding energy, which is the energy required to separate the components of the system. The greater the mass defect, the stronger the binding energy. When the components combine to form a bound system, the binding energy is released, and the system’s mass decreases as energy exits the system. In relativistic terms, the conservation of mass can be reframed as the conservation of a combination of energy and momentum, which remains invariant and provides the same invariant mass for any system, regardless of the observer. This principle also applies to particles created through pair production, where the invariant mass of a closed system remains unchanged even when new particles are formed.
